text.p: A sudden frost and a windfall of rebates from the taxman have lent seasonal cheer to sales at Finland's best-known department store Stockmann, the company said on Friday.

Hannu Penttila, director of the department store division said December domestic sales at Stockmann's department stores -- one of which is a landmark for visitors to the Finnish capital -- were six percent higher than last year at 315 million markka.
"It is a very good figure, clearly more than we expected," Penttila said in an interview.

Christmas sales got off to a sluggish start at the end of November and in early December, he said; but picked up clearly once Finland's winter frost set in and tax rebates landed on consumers' bank accounts.

"Christmas sales picked up considerably after the frost came since that created demand for heavy outdoor clothing and winter sports equipment," Penttila said. Helsinki temperatures around Christmas plunged to minus 20 Celsius (minus 4 Fahrenheit).

"Tax rebates helped as well," Penttila said, adding that it is estimated that most were spent on Christmas shopping. An annual rebate programme offers some relief to Finnish earners who pay an average of one-third of their income in tax.
Last year's hot sellers were mobile phones -- even though in Finland penetration is already high -- and computers, as well as snowboards which have more or less replaced ski sales, he said.

Stockmann seems to have continued to outperform its Finnish rivals -- the Federation of Finnish Commerce and Trade (KKL) has said total Christmas retail sales rose by 4.5 percent, to over three billion markka.
Christmas sales are significant for retailing everywhere: Penttila estimated that November-December business makes up roughly one-quarter of his division's annual total.

With demand picking up across Finland after a punishing recession in the early 1990s, Stockmann's full-year 1996 domestic department store sales showed brisk growth of nine percent to total 2.5 billion markka, Penttila said.
Another factor helping business is Helsinki's closeness to Russia -- with Communism defunct, wealthy Russians have recently become Stockmann's largest single group of tax-free shoppers.
"Russians tend to buy more expensive products such as furs, mobile phones, electronic equipment and winter sports equipment," said Penttila.
He estimated the Russian consumers' share of the company's total department store sales at around one to two percent.
On the whole, Penttila sees a bright year ahead for Stockmann with private consumption expected to pick-up 3.5 percent in 1997, according to official finance ministry figures.
"We have positive expectations for this year and we expect the department store division to perform at least on last year's level," he said.
Stockmann said with its first-half results in August that it expects the group's full-year 1996 profit before extraordinary items to at least match the 280 million markka booked in 1995.
